title: If God Hates Evil, Why Is He Still Letting Tomorrow Come?
paragraphs: If God Hates Evil, Why Is He Still Letting Tomorrow Come?

The terrifying answer to “Why doesn’t God end evil today?” is that the moment God finally removes every trace of rebellion from His creation, none of us gets to stand before Him pretending evil was only something other people did.
There is a question people whisper beside hospital beds.
They scream it over graves.
They ask it after watching another child suffer, another family collapse, another innocent person become somebody else’s victim.
Sometimes they ask it while staring at a ceiling at 3:17 in the morning because the person who hurt them is sleeping peacefully while they are still carrying what that person did.
And sometimes the question is much simpler.
“If God is good… why doesn’t He just end evil today?”
Not someday.
Not after another sermon.

Not after another generation of funerals, wars, abuse, trafficking, betrayal, cancer, murder, corruption, addiction, exploitation, and children learning far too young how cruel human beings can become.
Today.
If God is really God, why not stop it all before the sun rises tomorrow?
It sounds like an accusation.
But underneath it is often something else.
Pain.
And Scripture never requires wounded people to pretend that evil does not hurt.
The Bible contains people crying, “How long?”
The prophets grieved over injustice. The psalmists asked why wicked people seemed to prosper. Habakkuk looked at violence and demanded an answer from God.
And Jesus Himself stood outside the tomb of Lazarus and wept.
Christianity does not ask you to call evil good.
It tells you something far more astonishing:
God hates evil more than you do.
But that creates an uncomfortable question.
Why is it still here?
Maybe the answer begins with something most of us would rather not admit.
When we imagine God “ending evil,” we normally imagine Him ending the evil out there.
Stop the murderer.
Stop the abuser.
Stop the dictator.
Stop the trafficker.
Stop the corrupt official.
Stop the person who destroyed my family.
Stop the person who betrayed me.
Stop them.
And certainly, Scripture teaches that God will judge wickedness. Biblical Christianity offers no final universe in which cruelty simply gets away with everything.
But there is a problem.
Where exactly should God draw the line?
At murder?
Jesus took us deeper and confronted hatred.
At adultery?
Jesus confronted lust within the heart.
At theft?
What about greed?
At deception?
Then what happens to our lies?
At cruelty?
What about the words we used deliberately because we knew exactly where they would hurt?
At pride?
At envy?
At unforgiveness?
At selfishness?
At the secret sin nobody knows exists because we became very good at looking Christian in public?
Suddenly the question changes.
“God, why don't You destroy evil?”
becomes…
“God, when You destroy evil, what happens to the evil in me?”
That is where the question becomes frighteningly personal.
Scripture does not divide humanity into innocent people over here and evil people over there.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The religious.
The rebellious.
The respected.
The disgraced.
The person in prison and the person preaching behind a pulpit.
Sin differs terribly in its earthly consequences. Saying everyone is sinful does not mean every sin causes equal damage or that victims and perpetrators are morally interchangeable.
They are not.
Justice matters.
Victims matter.
Accountability matters.
But before the holiness of God, none of us can say, “There is absolutely no rebellion in me. Judge everyone else.”
And now we are getting dangerously close to the answer.
Peter wrote about people wondering why God's promised judgment seemed delayed.
His words in Greek are striking:
οὐ βραδύνει κύριος τῆς ἐπαγγελίας… ἀλλὰ μακροθυμεῖ εἰς ὑμᾶς
“The Lord is not slow concerning the promise… but is patient toward you.”
That word matters:
μακροθυμεῖ — makrothymei.
It carries the idea of patience, longsuffering, restraint.
God's apparent delay is not evidence that He has failed to notice evil.
Peter continues:
μὴ βουλόμενός τινας ἀπολέσθαι ἀλλὰ πάντας εἰς μετάνοιαν χωρῆσαι
“…not wishing any to perish, but all to come to repentance.” — 2 Peter 3:9.
Read that again.
What looks like delay can be mercy.
Tomorrow exists because repentance is still being offered.
That does not answer every philosophical question surrounding suffering. Christianity never gives us permission to explain every individual tragedy by casually announcing why God allowed it.
We often do not know.
But Scripture does tell us something about the apparent delay of final judgment.
God has appointed judgment.
And until that day, mercy is still calling sinners home.
Which means the frightening possibility is this:
You may have asked God why He hasn't judged the wicked yet…
while living inside the very mercy that has delayed judgment for you.
Think about Saul of Tarsus.
There was a time when Christians might reasonably have prayed for God to stop him.
Saul persecuted followers of Jesus. Acts tells us he approved of Stephen's death and ravaged the church.
Imagine being a Christian mother hearing that Saul was approaching your city.
You would not know Romans was coming.
You would not know Galatians was coming.
You would not know Philippians was coming.
You would not know that the persecutor would become the persecuted apostle proclaiming the Christ he once opposed.
You would only know that Saul was dangerous.
Then Jesus met him.
Grace interrupted his story.
The enemy became a brother.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The man Christians feared became a man willing to suffer for the name he once tried to silence.
What if God had answered someone's prayer for Saul by simply destroying Saul?
There would have been justice.
But there would not have been Paul's redemption.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly why that matters.
Because you have a past too.
Maybe yours was never public.
Maybe nobody made a documentary about your worst decisions.
Maybe your scandal never became gossip.
But you know.
You remember the version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever meets.
The addiction.
The affair.
The pornography.
The rage.
The dishonesty.
The years wasted.
The person you wounded.
The marriage you almost destroyed.
The secret double life.
The faith you abandoned.
The promises you made to God and broke before the week was over.
And perhaps you are still carrying something you cannot undo.
Listen carefully.
God's answer to evil was never pretending evil did not matter.
Look at the cross.
Christianity places at its center an innocent Man publicly tortured and executed.
Jesus does not minimize evil.
He enters the world where evil is happening.
He is betrayed.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Beaten.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
And from the darkness of Golgotha comes the staggering announcement of the Gospel:
God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
The cross tells us sin is worse than we imagined because redemption required the blood of Christ.
And the cross tells us God's love is greater than we imagined because Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
This is why Christianity cannot answer suffering with a cold sentence like, “Everything happens for a reason,” and then walk away.
The center of Christianity is not an explanation written on a chalkboard.
It is Jesus Christ hanging on a cross.
God entered suffering.
And then something happened on the third day.
The tomb opened.
Jesus rose.
And resurrection changed the ending.
That matters enormously when asking why evil continues today, because Christianity does not teach that evil continues forever.
God's patience has an expiration known to God.
Peter's very next words after describing God's patience warn that the Day of the Lord will come.
Justice delayed is not justice cancelled.
Scripture moves toward a day when Christ returns, evil is judged, death is defeated, and creation is made new.
Revelation gives us one of Scripture's most breathtaking promises: God will dwell with His people, wipe away their tears, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
Not managed.
Not temporarily reduced.
Gone.
The Bible's ending is not humanity escaping creation while evil wins.
It is God making all things new.
That means the Christian answer to evil has two words that must never be separated:
judgment and mercy.
If there were no final judgment, victims could reasonably ask whether evil ultimately mattered.
If there were no mercy, sinners like us would have no hope.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
And suddenly another thought becomes almost unbearable.
Every morning you wake up in a world where evil still exists is also a morning when the door of repentance has not yet closed.
The breath entering your lungs is mercy.
The heartbeat you barely notice is mercy.
Another opportunity to confess is mercy.
Another chance to forgive is mercy.
Another opportunity to make restitution where possible is mercy.
Another moment to turn from secret sin is mercy.
Another opportunity to surrender to Jesus Christ is mercy.
We keep asking:
“God, when will You finally do something about evil?”
And from Calvary comes the answer:
“I already have.”
And from the empty tomb:
“I am not finished.”
And from the promise of Christ's return:
“I will.”
Past.
Present.
Future.
At the cross, Jesus broke sin's claim upon everyone who belongs to Him.
Through His Spirit, He is transforming His people now.
At His return, evil and death will not have the final word.
So why doesn't God end evil today?
Part of the biblical answer is terrifyingly beautiful:
Because today is still a day of mercy.
Today another Saul can become Paul.
Today another prodigal can come home.
Today another addict can cry out for freedom.
Today another hypocrite can stop pretending.
Today another wounded believer can discover that suffering did not make Jesus abandon them.
Today another person who thought they were too dirty for God can discover what grace actually means.
Today…
maybe you.
And this is where this article stops being theology about somebody else.
What if God is giving you another day?
Not another day to hide.
Another day to come home.
You can fool followers.
You can fool family.
You can fool church people.
You can even learn enough Christian vocabulary to fool yourself.
But you cannot fool Jesus.
And strangely enough, that may be the best news you have heard all day.
Because the Christ who sees everything is still calling you.
Repentance in the New Testament is captured by the word μετάνοια — metanoia: repentance, a turning of mind and life toward God.
Not religious performance.
Not cleaning yourself up sufficiently so Jesus will finally tolerate you.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
Receive grace you could never purchase.
And then let that grace begin changing the places you once protected from God.
Maybe you have been furious because God has not ended the evil that wounded you.
Your wound matters.
Seeking justice is not a failure of faith.
Getting safe from an abusive situation is not rebellion against God.
Forgiveness does not require calling evil good, and reconciliation is not identical to forgiveness; trust may require genuine repentance, truth, safety, and time.
Jesus does not ask victims to pretend they were never wounded.
The risen Christ still carried scars.
Scars and resurrection occupied the same body.
Think about that.
Healing does not require pretending the wound never happened.
Jesus can redeem a story without rewriting history into something painless.
He does something greater.
He refuses to let evil write the final sentence.
That is Gospel Warrior's heartbeat:
Not because scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin didn't matter.
Not because suffering wasn't devastating.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He turns persecutors into apostles.
Prodigals into sons and daughters coming home.
Shame into testimony.
Bondage into freedom.
Condemnation into forgiveness.
Graves into resurrection ground.
And sinners into saints—not because they finally became impressive enough for God, but because Jesus saves.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished religious response.
Be honest.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another hurting person reading.
Then think of one person who has asked, “If God is real, why is there so much evil?”
Not for an algorithm.
For a person.
Send it privately to someone whose faith is hanging by a thread.
I want to say this carefully because biblical truth matters more than fundraising:
Salvation is by grace. Christian giving is to be willing rather than coerced; Paul says it should not be given “reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary financial generosity can genuinely be an act through which Christians honor God and help Gospel ministry continue.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Leave a meaningful comment.
Pray for the people who will read it.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is asking:
“Why hasn't God ended evil?”
Maybe what they do not yet realize is that the same God who promises to end evil is holding open the door of mercy right now.
And one day that door will no longer be called today.
So while it is today…
come home.
Not to religion.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Come to Jesus Christ.
The cross says your evil is serious.
The blood says forgiveness was costly.
The empty tomb says death is defeated.
God's patience says repentance is still possible.
And Christ's promised return says evil does not get the last word.
Maybe God hasn't ended the story yet because grace is still writing names into its final chapters.
And maybe tonight…
He is calling yours.
The world is waiting for God to end evil, while heaven is giving sinners one more day to run into the arms of Jesus.
